groups.name: What the semantics takes from outside
groups.plain: The frame: a theory of the physical world and of appraisal, taken as given, and the indices every claim is relative to.

groups.name: Things, their parts and their changes
groups.plain: Anything studied is a set of parts, each a constraint on some values, with a list of changes it admits.

groups.name: Questions and the changes they ask about
groups.plain: A question names a target, the changes it asks about, and what it asks; where the question came from is recorded.

groups.name: Telling parts apart by how they respond
groups.plain: Two parts are the same kind when every change the question admits affects them alike; nothing else makes a kind.

groups.name: The test of an explanation
groups.plain: Something counts as an account of a question when its parts match the target's parts, its answers match under every change, and the answers depend on its parts.

groups.name: Which parts do the work
groups.plain: Which parts, alone or together, an account cannot lose; and parts that do no work.

groups.name: Rivals, problems and tests
groups.plain: Two answers offered for one question that clash, that nobody can yet decide between, and the tests that can decide.

groups.name: Arguments, criticism and use
groups.plain: Reasons that rule things out for someone who can use them; criticism that has a target; premises taken as given.

groups.name: Where a correspondence came from
groups.plain: Every correspondence has a history: selected (variation and survival), constructed (worked out with a target in view), or only declared.

groups.name: Standing for something; prediction and surprise
groups.plain: A thing stands for something when a faithful correspondence with that history links them; prediction and surprise follow.

groups.name: Making something new
groups.plain: Building a new content inside the system, new against what it could already use, and used on a problem.

groups.name: Repair and created explanation
groups.plain: A repair of a stated aim, produced by a contribution; created explanation is a repair through a new account.

groups.name: Keeping a capability; the physical side
groups.plain: Tasks, keeping the ability to do them, owning that ability within a declared boundary, and the limits physics sets.

groups.name: Going on without limit, and the whole structure
groups.plain: Turning on one's own practice, universality, the classes, the commitments, and what would rule the semantics out.

groups.name: The text's own worked examples
groups.plain: The pole and its shadow, the balances, the tokens, the matrices, the two-layer episode and other worked cases.

avida_things.name: An Avida program, run alone or in the world
avida_things.plain: One instruction sequence running on Avida's simulated computer; its observed computational behaviour (copying, tasks).

avida_things.name: Instruction ablation
avida_things.plain: One instruction swapped for nop-X, an instruction that does nothing, and the program run again.

avida_things.name: Instruction changes when a program copies itself
avida_things.plain: Copying mistakes, and the one-in-twenty added or removed instruction at each split.

avida_things.name: The tasks, the rewards, and the code that checks them
avida_things.plain: The Avida execution environment's list of tasks and what each pays, written in a file in advance, and Avida's code that checks whether an output does a task.

avida_things.name: The numbers handed in, always in one order
avida_things.plain: The three numbers a program is handed, which the world always hands out in the same order.

avida_things.name: Changes to the world's own rules
avida_things.plain: What an instruction means changed (nand read as nor or and), the input channel removed, meanings shuffled.

avida_things.name: The program population and computational selection
avida_things.plain: Many programs copying themselves into a grid of 3,600 places; the ones that copy faster spread (Avida fitness).

avida_things.name: Program ancestry
avida_things.plain: The line of parent and descendant programs, thousands of generations long.

avida_things.name: The circuits read from Avida's records
avida_things.plain: The small wiring diagrams read from Avida's step-by-step records: the routes from the numbers handed in to the number handed out.

avida_things.name: Required and removable instructions
avida_things.plain: Which single instructions, pairs or triples had to be ablated for a task to stop while the copying went on.

avida_things.name: The six execution environments over time
avida_things.plain: Which environments made the program population do more tasks, and where the count stopped.

avida_things.name: Programs alike now, unlike after a change
avida_things.plain: Programs that do the same today and become different things after the same change.

avida_things.name: The people studying Avida
avida_things.plain: The owner's questions, Claude's plans written before running, the runs, the checks and their corrections. Not Avida itself.

avida_things.name: Nothing in Avida
avida_things.plain: Nothing in Avida, or in the Avida work, plays this part.

main_breaks.title: Whether an evolved program "stands for" its task, and counts as an explanation, flips on one unsettled reading
main_breaks.semantics: A correspondence that came about by variation and survival, with nothing in its history standing for the target, is "selected"; a selected, faithful correspondence "stands for" its target; and a candidate that passes the test of an explanation and is not merely declared is, by the semantics' sufficiency claim, an explanation.
main_breaks.avida: An Avida program that does a task, its program population, and Avida's own code that checks the task and pays for it.
main_breaks.happens: Computed in a copy of the semantics' own program: the program, taken as one block, passes all five conditions of the test of an explanation on the numbers the world hands in. If the code that checks the task is left out of the program's history, the program's correspondence is "selected", it stands for the task, and the semantics calls it an explanation. If that code counts as part of the history, the correspondence is "declared": it stands for nothing and is no explanation.
main_breaks.why: The semantics says a selected correspondence has nothing in its history that stands for the target, but in Avida the target is written down in advance, in the task list and the checking code, by people; whether that counts as "in the history" is a reading the text leaves open (the formal core marks it as invented).
main_breaks.example: The most common NOT program of run low seed 2 (110 instructions, 44 copies): it hands back nand(x, x), which is NOT x. Reading A: selected, represents NOT on the world's numbers, an explanation by the sufficiency claim, against the owner's reading of Avida as knowledge without the explanation kind. Reading B: declared, represents nothing, no explanation, which agrees with the owner and with the first Avida study.

main_breaks.title: Avida's "taking an instruction out" is not the semantics' "taking a part out"
main_breaks.semantics: Taking a part out (deletion) leaves the values it governed completely free; "required" parts are judged by that, and the semantics proves that taking parts out never removes a possibility.
main_breaks.avida: Instruction ablation: an instruction is swapped for one that does nothing, and the program is run again (the owner's "required instruction").
main_breaks.happens: The do-nothing instruction still does something definite: an ablated read leaves the next read to take its number. So Avida gives a definite, different answer where the semantics' deletion gives no answer at all, or no change; and in Avida a second ablation can bring back what a first one stopped, which deletion never can.
main_breaks.why: Ablation replaces an instruction with another instruction, a change of the program, while deletion removes all constraint; the owner's "required instruction" therefore lines up with the semantics' "a change at which the answer differs", not with the semantics' "a part the answer depends on".
main_breaks.example: In the most common EQU program of one run, ablating an unused read at instruction 45 made the reads at 47, 53 and 66 receive the third, second and first numbers instead of the first, third and second, and EQU was gone. In 85 of 89 hard cases one ablation stopped the copying and a second one restored it.

main_breaks.title: The earlier answer to "what is it?", the circuit, fails the semantics' test of an explanation
main_breaks.semantics: An account of a question must give the target's answer at every change the question asks about (question fidelity), not most of them.
main_breaks.avida: The circuits read from Avida's records, offered earlier as "what that evolved information actually is", and the single ablations made in the same study.
main_breaks.happens: Read as an explanation of "does the program still do the task after this one ablation?", the circuit says "it stops" exactly when the ablated instruction lies on every route. Over 83,725 program-task pairs it is wrong at only 5.4 in 100 of the 7.15 million ablations, but right at every ablation in only 8.8 in 100 pairs: 17 in 100 for NOT, 0 for XOR and EQU.
main_breaks.why: Some required instructions are not on the circuit (markers, extra reads that shift the numbers, jumps), and some instructions on the circuit are not required (another route takes over); the circuit describes the path the numbers took, not how the program responds to every change.
main_breaks.example: The NOT/EQU program of run low seed 2: for EQU, six required instructions lie off the circuit (23, 26, 27, 29, 31, 67) and four on the circuit are not required (11, 51, 74, 95).

main_breaks.title: In Avida, lasting does not require doing the task
main_breaks.semantics: A selected correspondence "survives" by being faithful on the changes it met: the survival condition requires fidelity.
main_breaks.avida: Computational selection: programs that do a rewarded task get more running time and spread; programs that do none still copy themselves and last.
main_breaks.happens: Whole program populations last 50,000 updates doing almost no task when nothing pays, and in every environment many programs last without doing the rewarded task.
main_breaks.why: Avida's selection is a graded advantage (a faster rate of copying), not a pass-or-fail condition; doing the task pays better, it is not required.
main_breaks.example: The environment that pays for nothing, run 1: after 50,000 updates, 3,600 programs, of which 11 do NOT. The fixed-list environment, run 1: 3,595 programs, 2,290 do NOT.
main_breaks.under_S83_and_S84: Decided by S84. A graded advantage counts: where doing the task raised a program's rate of copying, the program survived on its history; in the run that paid for nothing, doing NOT changed nothing, and the 11 programs doing NOT there are not selected for NOT (MC1b: Sel false with the graded condition, true without it). The break stays as a fact about Avida (lasting does not require the task) and no longer stops the semantics' definition applying.

main_breaks.title: Everything about explanation as an activity has nothing in Avida
main_breaks.semantics: Problems (two answers nobody can yet decide between), arguments and criticism, rivals offered one in place of another, recognized difficulties, construction, origin, deployment, created explanation, turning on one's own practice.
main_breaks.avida: Nothing. The nearest things are the world withholding reward (a signal, not a criticism), programs competing for room (not rivals), and copying mistakes (not conjectures).
main_breaks.happens: Of the semantics' units about these, none has an Avida counterpart that meets its conditions; every one that has a near counterpart fails a condition.
main_breaks.why: No Avida program holds a problem, states or uses a claim, compares versions, or has anything that stands for something outside it in a way it can use; all the choosing is done by the execution environment, and all the asking, testing and criticising by the people studying Avida.
main_breaks.example: One of Astra's designs: programs give running time to a neighbour or not, depending on a number the neighbour sends; after 5,000 updates 76 to 88 in 100 gave to nobody. A choice about another program, carried by instructions, with no problem, no reason and no criticism behind it.
main_breaks.refs: L315, L383, L429; S111 section 8; decision S63

main_breaks.title: Avida's "learning new things" is, in the semantics' words, selection, not creation
main_breaks.semantics: New means not matching anything the system could already deploy on a problem; origin needs a construction inside the system; creativity lives in construction.
main_breaks.avida: The new capabilities of the six-environment study: tasks no program in the run did before, appearing over thousands of updates.
main_breaks.happens: Every new capability came by copying mistakes that lasted (the semantics' selection response). Since nothing in Avida deploys anything on a problem, the semantics' "repertoire" is empty and its "new" holds of everything and says nothing; its "origin" is never met.
main_breaks.why: The semantics measures newness against usable understanding and asks for construction; Avida has variation and selection only.
main_breaks.example: Growing list, run 1: 65 tasks commonly done at the end, every one "new" in the study's sense, none an origin in the semantics' sense; the one run let go on stayed at 41 for 25,000 more updates.
main_breaks.refs: D13.5 line 518; L13, L225, L413-L422; S113 section 4; S116 section 4

main_breaks.title: Programs fail where the world never looks, but nothing in Avida is surprised
main_breaks.semantics: Surprise is a selected correspondence failing at a change it was never shaped against, when that change occurs; it needs a layer that predicts.
main_breaks.avida: The one order in which the world hands out its numbers, and the tests in this job that handed the same numbers in the other five orders.
main_breaks.happens: In 16 of 18 saved program populations some programs that do NOT in the world's order fail in another order while others do not: the exact shape of surprise. But Avida programs predict nothing, and the world never changes its order, so the failure never happens to them; only the tests show it.
main_breaks.why: Surprise in the semantics needs a predicting layer and an occurring change; Avida has neither.
main_breaks.example: Growing-list run 2: 2,370 programs do NOT in the world's order; handed the same numbers with the second and third swapped, 34 of them still do and 2,336 do not.

main_breaks.title: Avida's simulated world is exact; the semantics' physics never is
main_breaks.semantics: No performance or retention tolerance is ever exact.
main_breaks.avida: Avida's simulated computer: the same program on the same numbers always gives the same answer.
main_breaks.happens: The semantics' tolerances have no counterpart in Avida's world: every performance there is exact.
main_breaks.why: Avida's "physics" is a program; the semantics' physical module is a theory of the physical world.
main_breaks.example: 23,332 programs were followed step by step against Avida's own record with no difference anywhere.

reverse_list.name: Copying itself
reverse_list.what: A program whose own instructions make copies of it (15 of the first program's 100 instructions do it). The semantics speaks of copying only as something done to a content; it has no term for a content that causes its own copying, the owner's first property.

reverse_list.name: Withstanding change by arrangement
reverse_list.what: 69 to 79 in 100 one-instruction changes leave an evolved program still copying; programs evolved with more copying mistakes lose less. The semantics can compute where a change breaks an account (its "boundary" over a family of changes) but has no term for how much of the family a thing withstands.

reverse_list.name: Lasting by out-copying removal
reverse_list.what: In Avida a program lasts only by being copied faster than the world removes programs. The semantics has continuity and retention, but no term for persistence as a balance of copying and removal.

reverse_list.name: A graded advantage
reverse_list.what: Avida fitness is a rate that decides which program spreads, not a pass-or-fail condition; the semantics has no score, rate or ordering of anything.

reverse_list.name: How widespread a capability is
reverse_list.what: The studies count tasks "present" (one program) and "common" (one in ten); the semantics has no population-level quantity.

reverse_list.name: Pay that falls as more programs use it
reverse_list.what: The "common sums pay less" environment pays from a store that runs down. The semantics has no term for an aim whose worth depends on how many already meet it.

reverse_list.name: An order in which questions are posed
reverse_list.what: The growing list added harder tasks as easier ones became common, and ended with more than the environment that offered all 77 at once. The semantics records a question's origin, but has no term for the order in which declared questions are presented.

reverse_list.name: What a program can become next
reverse_list.what: Two programs that do the same now become different things after the same change. The semantics separates them (two systems with the same outputs can be different organizations) but has no term for a thing's reach under further variation.

reverse_list.name: A cost borne for another
reverse_list.what: Programs that give running time to a neighbour at a cost to themselves. The semantics has no term for one system's cost for another's benefit.

readings_in_S117.A: The code in Avida that checks a task is not an occurrence, in the history that selected a program, that represents the survival condition or the task (it belongs to the world's rules).
readings_in_S117.B: That code is such an occurrence: it was written by people and computes the task, so it represents the task and the survival condition, earlier than the program that holds the correspondence.
readings_in_S117.where_the_text_leaves_it_open: D12.1 (formal core line 454): "No member of the history represents t, H, or the survival condition"; the formal core marks the reading of "member of the history" as occurrences as invented (I52) and h(t) as "the history that produced that holding, its preparing episode included" (I167). Whether Avida's task-checking code is in h(t) is not settled by the text, nor here.

decisions.S83: Reading C ("Oh clearly C."): the history in the definition of a selected correspondence (D12.1) is read inside the system boundary declared for the claim. With the owner's boundary (S72: the whole Avida execution environment is the selector), the task-checking code, written by people outside that boundary, stands for nothing inside it, so an evolved program's correspondence with its task can be selected; at a boundary that takes in Avida's authors it is declared (B's verdict). Written into copies only: tests/129, and results/S129 Reading C carried into copies/.
decisions.S84: Being copied more often counts as surviving ("Well yes. That is how selected is defined."): D12.1's survival condition asks that fidelity on the history changes which members persist or are copied. Written into the same copies.
